caseStudies.ctaTitle: If any of this sounds familiar
caseStudies.ctaDesc: Tell us what is costing you time. We reply within one business day.
caseStudies.cs1Challenge: An operations team managing complex programme delivery was spending over 60% of staff time on manual data entry, report compilation, and cross-referencing records across multiple spreadsheets. The process was error-prone, slow, and preventing the team from focusing on core delivery work.
caseStudies.cs1Solution: We deployed a document processing AI pipeline that automatically extracts, validates, and categorises incoming reports and records. An n8n workflow routes data into the correct Airtable bases and triggers summary reports for programme managers, without any manual intervention.
caseStudies.cs1Result1: 78% reduction in manual data processing time
caseStudies.cs1Result3: Error rate dropped from 8% to under 0.5%
caseStudies.cs1Result4: Programme managers receive auto-generated weekly summaries
caseStudies.cs2Challenge: A mid-sized consulting firm was manually processing client invoices, reconciling expenses, and generating monthly financial reports. Three members of the finance team spent an average of 2 days per month solely on invoice reconciliation. With a growing client base, this was becoming unsustainable.
caseStudies.cs2Solution: We built a fully automated invoice processing system that ingests invoices via email, extracts line items using document AI, validates against purchase orders in their ERP, and posts approved invoices directly to Xero. A Slack notification alerts the finance lead only when human review is required.
caseStudies.cs2Result2: Invoice processing time cut from 2 days to 90 minutes/month
caseStudies.cs2Result3: 94% of invoices processed without human intervention
caseStudies.cs2Result4: Finance team reallocated to higher-value client work
caseStudies.cs3Challenge: A logistics operation was losing competitive advantage due to a slow invoicing cycle. Invoices were manually compiled from multiple driver reports, fuel logs, and delivery confirmations, a process taking 3 full working days per billing cycle. Late invoices were causing cash flow problems and client dissatisfaction.
caseStudies.cs3Solution: We integrated all data sources, driver apps, GPS systems, fuel cards, and delivery confirmation data, into a unified pipeline. An AI agent compiles draft invoices automatically, flags exceptions, and sends approved invoices to clients via the existing billing system. The entire cycle now runs overnight.
caseStudies.cs3Result1: Invoice cycle compressed from 3 days to 4 hours
caseStudies.cs3Result2: Cash flow improved by approximately 18 days per quarter
caseStudies.cs3Result3: Zero manual compilation for 91% of invoices

about.metaDesc: Fifteen years of being responsible for systems businesses had to rely on. Maxpromo Digital came out of that.
about.title: Fifteen years of being responsible when it had to keep running.
about.intro: Maxpromo Digital designs and builds the systems companies run on, and keeps running them afterwards. The second part is what decides whether the first part was worth doing.
about.storyBody: Joomla, WordPress, Drupal and TYPO3. Shared hosting and self-managed servers. SQL, migrations, backups and the imports that go wrong at two in the morning. Fifteen years of that is what informs how we build now: cautiously, with a way back, and with someone responsible when it breaks.
about.transformTitle: Most businesses do not need another website.
about.transformBody: They need the tools they already pay for to talk to each other. They need the manual steps gone. They need the old system brought up to a state somebody can work with. A rebuild is sometimes the answer. More often it is the expensive way to avoid a smaller and less comfortable question about how the work moves.

principles.d: We do not start from a technology and look for somewhere to put it. We start from what is costing time and work back.
A smaller system a team actually uses beats a larger one that impresses in a demo and is abandoned by March.

principles.t: A person stays in the loop
principles.d: Anything that leaves the business is drafted and approved. Automation prepares work. It does not act on your behalf unsupervised.
A system nobody maintains decays. We keep running what we build, or hand it over properly to someone who will.

about.arcLede: Nobody starts out designing the systems a business runs on. You end up there after years of being the person answerable for whether something kept working.
about.a1Body: Production environments, databases, migrations, hosting, integrations. An import that went wrong at two in the morning and a business that has to trade again by nine. Years of that, for real companies with real customers.
about.a2Body: Almost never at the technology. Systems break at the edges: where information gets carried from one place to the next, where nobody owns the handover, where one person holds it all in their head and then takes a holiday.
about.a3Body: Once you know where it breaks, the question changes. It stops being which tool, and becomes how does the work actually run here, and which of these steps should not need to exist.
about.a4Label: Building the systems a business runs on
about.a4Body: That is what Maxpromo Digital became. We design the route work takes through a company and build the systems that carry it. A business should get easier to run as it grows, not harder.

founder.title: Fifteen years of keeping business systems running, and now building what comes next.
founder.p1: I’m Marcel Akwe. For more than fifteen years I have worked with websites, content management systems, databases, hosting and the business software around them, usually as the person who had to keep it running.
founder.p2: That work now reaches into automation, AI, agents and connected business operations. The tools have changed. The questions I start with have not:
founder.l1: Where does the information come from?
founder.l2: Who touches it, and where does it wait?
founder.l3: What needs a decision, and who makes it?
founder.p3: Maxpromo Digital is deliberately small. The person you talk to first is the person responsible for what gets built.
founder.p4: The rule has stayed the same the whole time:
founder.rule: Understand the business before choosing the technology.

whatWeDo.d3: Sometimes a handful of steps repeat every day and should be carrying themselves.

whatWeDo.s2Body: What arrives, who touches it, where it waits, what gets copied, what needs a decision.
whatWeDo.s3Title: We say what we would change first
whatWeDo.s3Body: Including when the answer is that you do not need us, or need less than you thought.
whatWeDo.closeTitle: What is taking too much time in your business?
whatWeDo.closeBody: You do not need to know what system you need. Tell us what is happening now.
whatWeDo.closeCta: Tell us what is slowing you down
whatWeDo.aosTitle: Sometimes one workflow is enough. Sometimes it isn’t.
whatWeDo.aosIntro: Not every problem needs a new application. And not every problem can be fixed with one automation.
whatWeDo.aosABody: Useful when one clear, repetitive task needs to move faster or more reliably.
whatWeDo.aosBBody: Useful when several people, tools and decisions need to work from the same process.
aosBFit: people need different views or permissions
the current tools no longer fit the process
whatWeDo.aosBridge1: We don’t start by deciding which one to sell you.

capabilityPages.c1AfterA11y: After: the enquiry is captured once, routed automatically, prepared for a person to approve, and recorded in one place.
capabilityPages.c1BeforeA11y: Before: an enquiry arrives and is handled by five separate manual steps, with information copied between them and no single record.
capabilityPages.c1CtaBody: The part of the week that feels like typing rather than working is usually the right place to start.
capabilityPages.c1FamiliarLede: Not every business does all of these. Most recognise two or three.
capabilityPages.c1FamiliarTitle: A day is full of small steps nobody planned.
capabilityPages.c1HumanBody: A quote going out, a price being agreed, an exception to the usual rule. Those stay with the person whose job they are. What changes is that the work arrives ready for the decision instead of needing to be assembled first.
capabilityPages.c1HumanTitle: The system does the carrying. People still decide.
capabilityPages.c1Lede: Most of the work we automate is not complicated. It is just repeated. The same details typed into a second system, the same message written again, the same document prepared the same way every time.
capabilityPages.c1MeansLede: In practice it is a short list of unglamorous things, done reliably.
capabilityPages.c1MeansTitle: Automation is not the same as making everything autonomous.
capabilityPages.c1Title: Stop moving the same information by hand.
capabilityPages.c1f1: An enquiry arrives and someone retypes it somewhere else.
capabilityPages.c1f2: A message sits unread because it landed in the wrong place.
capabilityPages.c1f3: A spreadsheet is updated after the fact so the numbers still line up.
capabilityPages.c1f4: A document is prepared by hand from information that already exists.
capabilityPages.c1f5: Somebody has to remember to follow up, and sometimes nobody does.
capabilityPages.c1f6: A status is copied into a second tool so the rest of the team can see it.
capabilityPages.c1m1Body: The information is entered a single time, wherever it first arrives.
capabilityPages.c1m2Body: It reaches the right person or the right system without being forwarded by hand.
capabilityPages.c1m3Body: Documents, replies and records are drafted from what is already known.
capabilityPages.c1m4Body: What happened is written down where the business can find it later.
capabilityPages.c1m5Body: Anything that commits the business to something waits for somebody to approve it.
capabilityPages.c1m5Title: Leave the decision with a person
capabilityPages.c2BuildTitle: One focused place where the work actually happens.
capabilityPages.c2Cta: Tell us what you have outgrown
capabilityPages.c2CtaBody: Usually there is one process everybody complains about. That is the one to describe.
capabilityPages.c2CtaTitle: Tell us what you have outgrown.
capabilityPages.c2FamiliarLede: Again, not all of these. Two of them is usually enough to be worth a conversation.
capabilityPages.c2FamiliarTitle: The software is still in use, and so are the workarounds.
capabilityPages.c2HonestBody: It is more to build, more to look after and more to get wrong. Often the right move is to connect the systems you already have, or to use more of what you already pay for. We will say so when that is the case, and it costs you less than the alternative.
capabilityPages.c2HonestClose: Building something new is worth it when the process is genuinely yours, and the software you can buy is built for a different business.
capabilityPages.c2HonestTitle: Custom software is not automatically the better answer.
capabilityPages.c2HumanBody: An application that forces a new way of working gets abandoned, and the spreadsheets come back. We start from what people do now, keep the parts that work, and only change what is causing the trouble.
capabilityPages.c2HumanTitle: Built around how your team already works.
capabilityPages.c2Lede: Most businesses do not outgrow their software all at once. It happens gradually, and the signs are familiar long before anyone calls it a problem.
capabilityPages.c2Title: When spreadsheets and off-the-shelf software stop fitting.
capabilityPages.c2b1Body: The screen your team works in all day, built around the process they actually follow.
capabilityPages.c2b2Body: A place for customers, suppliers or staff to do one thing without an email thread.
capabilityPages.c2b3Body: Jobs, records, approvals and status in one place instead of four.
capabilityPages.c2b4Body: A front end for an automated process, so people can see it and step in.
capabilityPages.c2f1: There are more spreadsheets than anyone can name, and some of them matter.
capabilityPages.c2f2: An important process lives mostly in one person's head.
capabilityPages.c2f3: Staff have quiet workarounds for the software they were given.
capabilityPages.c2f4: The same information exists in three places and disagrees in at least one.
capabilityPages.c2f5: The tool technically supports the task, but only through steps nobody would design.
capabilityPages.c2f6: Customers or staff need one focused place to do a thing, and there isn't one.
capabilityPages.c3BuildTitle: The site as the first step of a process, not the end of one.
capabilityPages.c3Cta: Show us what your website is not doing
capabilityPages.c3CtaBody: The most useful question is what happens after the form is submitted. If the answer involves several people and some retyping, there is something there worth having.
capabilityPages.c3CtaTitle: Show us what your website is not doing.
capabilityPages.c3FamiliarEyebrow: Does any of this sound familiar?
capabilityPages.c3FamiliarLede: As always, not all of it. Two of these is usually enough to see where the site stops helping.
capabilityPages.c3FamiliarTitle: The site is finished. The work behind it is not.
capabilityPages.c3HonestBody: They need the one they have to do something. A rebuild is the most visible intervention and rarely the most effective: it takes months, changes nothing about the work behind it, and is usually justified on the grounds that the old site is no longer to anyone's taste.
capabilityPages.c3HonestClose: A rebuild earns its place when the site is technically finished, when it can no longer be maintained, or when the process behind it has to be rethought anyway. Otherwise the better intervention is often small and invisible.
capabilityPages.c3HonestTitle: Most businesses do not need a new website.
capabilityPages.c3HumanBody: An automatic acknowledgement is useful. An automatic reply to a complaint is not. What the site takes on is sorting, passing along and recording. What a person takes on is everything the sender wanted a person for.
capabilityPages.c3Lede: Most company websites are brochures with a contact form. They look tidy and take nothing off anybody's desk. It gets interesting where the site does not merely accept an enquiry but passes it on in a shape nobody has to retype.
capabilityPages.c3Title: A website should do some of the work.
capabilityPages.c3b1Body: A form that asks enough to place the enquiry and little enough that it gets sent. What comes in lands where the work happens, not only in an inbox.
capabilityPages.c3b2Body: A billing question and an emergency do not belong in the same queue. The site can tell them apart before a person reads either one.
capabilityPages.c3b3Body: Opening hours, process, who is responsible, rough price. Not buried in a legal page but where the question occurs. Every question the site answers is one phone call fewer.
capabilityPages.c3b4Body: The site is rarely the only system. It becomes useful when it tells the rest, instead of being one more island.
capabilityPages.c3b4Title: A connection to what you already run
capabilityPages.c3f1: An enquiry arrives through a form and is then typed by hand into something else.
capabilityPages.c3f2: Nobody is quite sure what happened to an enquiry after the confirmation email went out.
capabilityPages.c3f3: The same questions keep arriving, even though the answer is on the site, just not where anyone looks.
capabilityPages.c3f4: The form either asks too little to be useful or so much that nobody completes it.
capabilityPages.c3f5: There is no difference between an urgent enquiry and a casual one.
capabilityPages.c3f6: The site was built years ago, and every change costs an agency and a fortnight.
capabilityPages.c4Cta: Tell us what keeps not getting said
capabilityPages.c4CtaBody: There is usually one story everyone inside the business knows and nobody outside it does. That is where we start.
capabilityPages.c4CtaTitle: Tell us what you meant to say.
capabilityPages.c4FamiliarEyebrow: Does any of this sound familiar?
capabilityPages.c4FamiliarLede: Two of these is usually enough to see where it stops.
capabilityPages.c4HonestBody: The problem is the capturing. Build a system that generates text but does not record what actually happened during the work and you get a great deal of content with nothing in it. It shows in the writing, and it shows to the reader.
capabilityPages.c4HonestClose: It becomes useful when the capturing happens where the work happens, and the preparing comes after. In that order.
capabilityPages.c4HonestTitle: The problem is rarely the writing.
capabilityPages.c4HumanBody: A model can write a draft. It cannot know which customer is annoyed this week, which phrasing lands badly locally, or which subject is the wrong one right now. So every flow ends at an approval here, and at one somebody actually reads.
capabilityPages.c4HumanTitle: The machine prepares. How the business sounds is your decision.
capabilityPages.c4Lede: In most businesses publishing does not fail for lack of ideas. It fails because there are seven steps between “that would be interesting” and “that is out”, and nobody owns them.
capabilityPages.c4Title: You have things worth saying. You just did not want a second full-time job.
capabilityPages.c4b1Body: One place a note from the working day lands before it is forgotten. Two sentences is enough; completeness is somebody else's job later.
capabilityPages.c4b2Body: What was captured becomes a draft, not a finished post. A draft that already knows what happened is a different thing entirely from an empty box.
capabilityPages.c4b3Body: A person decides whether this goes out. Who that is, and how you can tell something was released, is settled before anything is automated.
capabilityPages.c4b4Body: What was published stays findable, with its reason and its date. Otherwise the same story gets told again in eighteen months, slightly differently.
capabilityPages.c4f1: There is a profile where nothing has happened for months.
capabilityPages.c4f2: Good stories happen during the work and disappear again, because nobody writes them down.
capabilityPages.c4f3: When something needs publishing, somebody starts from an empty box.
capabilityPages.c4f4: The approval route is unclear, so to be safe nobody publishes.
capabilityPages.c4f5: The same thing gets rewritten three times for three channels.
capabilityPages.c4f6: Nobody knows what was already said six months ago.
capabilityPages.c5BuildTitle: One place that leads, and channels that follow it.
capabilityPages.c5Cta: Show us what gets maintained twice
capabilityPages.c5CtaBody: The most useful question is this: if a price changes tomorrow, in how many places does somebody have to act?
capabilityPages.c5CtaTitle: Show us what gets maintained more than once.
capabilityPages.c5FamiliarEyebrow: Does any of this sound familiar?
capabilityPages.c5FamiliarTitle: The details are right. Just not everywhere at once.
capabilityPages.c5HonestBody: It is a question-of-ownership problem. Until it is settled which place leads for a product detail, every integration just moves the contradiction somewhere new and harder to see.
capabilityPages.c5HonestClose: Making that decision costs one conversation. Avoiding it costs continuously.
capabilityPages.c5HonestTitle: This is rarely a shop problem.
capabilityPages.c5HumanBody: A system may distribute details and report contradictions. What something costs, what is promised and when an exception is made belongs to people who know the customer and the margin. Automatic price changes without a release are exactly the kind of convenience that ends up expensive.
capabilityPages.c5HumanTitle: Prices and promises stay your decision.
capabilityPages.c5Lede: As soon as a product sells through more than one channel, every change becomes a small project: price, description, image, availability, each in several places, each by hand.
capabilityPages.c5Title: A product detail should not need maintaining in five places.
capabilityPages.c5b1Body: A place that is authoritative even while several systems stay in use. Leading does not mean only.
capabilityPages.c5b2Body: A price or description change is made once and travels to where it is needed, instead of waiting in somebody's task list.
capabilityPages.c5b3Body: Availability, status and disagreements presented so that a wrong detail is noticed before a customer finds it.
capabilityPages.c5b4Body: The path from order to done as one process with a visible state, rather than a chain of individual handoffs.
capabilityPages.c5f1: A price changed, and somewhere the old one is still showing.
capabilityPages.c5f2: Which place holds the authoritative product detail is a matter of opinion.
capabilityPages.c5f3: Launching a product means doing the same work again, once per channel.
capabilityPages.c5f4: Availability is updated afterwards rather than carried along, and sometimes too late.
capabilityPages.c5f5: After an order there is a chain of forwards and shouted questions.
capabilityPages.c5f6: Nobody can say what is selling where without asking somebody.
capabilityPages.c1ProofAlt: Our quotation system after reading a customer email: the form filled in, review notes listing what could not be confirmed, and a preview with three positions.
capabilityPages.c1ProofNote: Our own quotation system, after reading an ordinary customer email: the form is filled in, the system lists what it could not confirm, and nothing is saved until a person decides. Shown in a controlled test environment with an invented customer.
capabilityPages.c2ProofAlt: The invoice list of our own back office application, showing one invoice sent and one paid.
capabilityPages.c2ProofNote: The application we run our own business on: quotations, invoices and customers in one place, built around how we work. Shown in a controlled test environment with an invented customer.
capabilityPages.c2ProofLink: See how a quotation is made in it
capabilityPages.c1Route: This page is about one clear workflow at a time. If the work itself has outgrown the tools, start with custom applications instead.
capabilityPages.c1RouteLink: How we tell an automation from a system
capabilityPages.c2Route: This page is about work that has outgrown its tools. If one clear, repetitive workflow is the problem, workflow automation is usually enough.
capabilityPages.c2RouteLink: How we tell a system from an automation

frictionCheck.ctaBody: Tell us how the work actually happens today. We will tell you what can be simplified, what can be connected, and what should stay exactly as it is.
frictionCheck.ctaNoEmail: The result above stands on its own. Only its category goes with you to the contact form, not your answers.
frictionCheck.ctaTitle: Want us to look at it with you?
frictionCheck.disclaimer: This result is based only on your six answers. It is an orientation, not an analysis of your business, and it measures nothing.
frictionCheck.disconnectedFirst: Decide on one place where a job authoritatively stands, even while information keeps arriving through different channels. Merging the channels is rarely realistic; a shared state is.
frictionCheck.disconnectedLooks: What belongs to one job sits in several places: email, a spreadsheet, a messenger, a note. Anyone who needs to know something first needs to know where to look.
frictionCheck.disconnectedWatch: The expensive part is not the searching. It is what nobody finds. Scattered information and missed follow-up almost always travel together.
frictionCheck.documentsFirst: Look at the last ten. If nine follow the same structure, this is a preparation problem rather than a writing problem: the system can prepare the draft, and a person still decides.
frictionCheck.documentsLooks: Quotations, confirmations and invoices get made by copying and adjusting. That is quick while nothing unusual is involved, and expensive the moment something is.
frictionCheck.documentsWatch: Preparing is not sending. Who checks the draft and who releases it should be exactly as clear after automation as it was before.
frictionCheck.followUpFirst: The first question is not the reminder, it is the list: is there an authoritative view of what is open at all? Without one, a system has nothing to remind you about.
frictionCheck.followUpLooks: Open items sit until the customer gets in touch. That costs no visible effort. It costs work that never arrives.
frictionCheck.followUpWatch: Automatic follow-up without context damages customer relationships faster than no follow-up does. The reason has to be right, not just the timing.
frictionCheck.learnBody: What should be automated first, and what is better left with people.
frictionCheck.lede: Six questions about things that happen in an ordinary week. At the end you see what kind of friction your business has and what to do about it first. No score, no rating, no email required.
frictionCheck.meta: About four minutes. You see the result immediately.
frictionCheck.q1: A new enquiry arrives. Where does it land?
frictionCheck.q1a: In one place everyone can see
frictionCheck.q1b: In an inbox, and someone forwards it
frictionCheck.q1c: Sometimes email, sometimes WhatsApp, sometimes a note
frictionCheck.q2: A quotation or order confirmation gets made. How?
frictionCheck.q2a: Mostly automatically, from information we already hold
frictionCheck.q2b: Copy an old one and change it
frictionCheck.q2c: Retype it from an email or a note
frictionCheck.q2d: Someone has to go and gather the details first
frictionCheck.q3: Before something goes to a customer, who checks it?
frictionCheck.q3a: One person, and it happens quickly
frictionCheck.q3b: One person, who is often unavailable
frictionCheck.q4: An enquiry is still open. How does the follow-up happen?
frictionCheck.q4c: We notice when the customer chases us
frictionCheck.q4d: Sometimes it does not happen at all
frictionCheck.q5: Typing the same information into more than one tool?
frictionCheck.q5d: Constantly, it is a fixed part of the job
frictionCheck.q6: Someone asks how far along a job is. How do you find out?
frictionCheck.q6a: Look it up, it is in one place
frictionCheck.repeatedWorkFirst: Do not automate it yet. First write down where each piece of information is created and where it travels afterwards. Half the duplication often disappears once that order is settled.
frictionCheck.repeatedWorkLooks: The same information gets typed in more than once, because the tools know nothing about each other. It rarely registers as a problem, because it is spread across the day.
frictionCheck.repeatedWorkWatch: Duplicate entry also produces contradictory records. When two systems show different numbers, the question is not which is right but which one leads.
frictionCheck.startNote: Answer how things actually run, not how they should run. Otherwise the result describes a business that does not exist.
frictionCheck.title: Where does the working week snag?
frictionCheck.waitingFirst: Start by asking which decisions genuinely need an approval. Some of them need one for historical reasons rather than real ones. What remains can be made visible instead of sitting in an inbox.
frictionCheck.waitingLooks: Work stops while somebody waits for an approval, a piece of information or a reply. That waiting appears in no report.
frictionCheck.waitingWatch: Removing approvals is not the goal. Some decisions belong to a person. They simply should not depend on whether somebody sees an email in time.
frictionCheck.nothingUrgentBody: Your answers don’t point to a major operational bottleneck right now. That is useful to know. We would not recommend automating work simply because it can be automated.
frictionCheck.nothingUrgentNext: Keep an eye on the tasks that start taking more time as the business grows.
frictionCheck.simplifyBody: There are signs that part of the work has become more complicated than it needs to be. Before adding technology, the process itself is worth simplifying.
frictionCheck.simplifyNext: Start with the step that creates the most waiting, copying or confusion.
frictionCheck.automationBody: You have repetitive work with a reasonably clear pattern. That is often where a focused automation can remove manual effort without changing the whole business.
frictionCheck.automationNext: Show us the repeated task and the tools involved.
frictionCheck.systemBody: The friction appears to span several tools, people or stages of work. Another isolated automation may only move the problem. It may be worth looking at the process as one connected system.
frictionCheck.systemNext: Walk us through how the work happens today.
frictionCheck.sawTitle: What we saw in your answers

automationGuide.closeAlt: Or just tell us how the work happens today.
automationGuide.closeBody: The Business Friction Check asks six questions about things that happen in an ordinary week and names the kind of friction your business has. No score, no email required, and it is allowed to conclude that there is nothing to do right now.
automationGuide.closeTitle: If you are not sure where you stand
automationGuide.lede: Most businesses automate the wrong thing first: the one that annoys them loudest. The more useful question is which kinds of work are suited to it at all, and which are better left with people.
automationGuide.m1Body: The task everyone complains about is often rare and complicated. The task that costs four minutes a day and nobody mentions is usually the better place to start.
automationGuide.m2Body: Some processes are complicated because a decision was never made. Automation then gets used to keep avoiding it, and makes it more expensive to make later.
automationGuide.m3Body: After automation it has to be clear who notices when it stops working. A silent failure nobody spots for three weeks is worse than the manual work it replaced.
automationGuide.o1: Duplicate entry that happens daily. Most certain benefit, lowest risk.
automationGuide.o2: One shared record of what is open. Fixes searching and following up at the same time.
automationGuide.o3: Document preparation for the ordinary case, with a person releasing it.
automationGuide.o4: Reminders about open items, driven by a reason rather than only a schedule.
automationGuide.o5: Integration between two systems that need to know the same thing.
automationGuide.orderLede: When several things qualify, this order helps. It is not sorted by effort but by how certain the benefit is.
automationGuide.orderNote: If an exception springs to mind immediately against one of these, that is not an obstacle. It is the information that this one should be simplified first and automated second.
automationGuide.readingTime: About eight minutes to read. None of it assumes you will work with us.
automationGuide.rule1Ask: Before automating anything, ask: if we simply removed this step, what would break? For a surprising number of steps the honest answer is nothing.
automationGuide.rule1Body: Automating an awkward process does not make it better. It makes it awkward faster, and harder to change afterwards. Automate an approval step that exists for historical reasons and you have just cast it in concrete for five years.
automationGuide.rule2Ask: For one single job, write down where each piece of information is first created and where it travels next. Half a page is usually enough, and it is usually uncomfortable reading.
automationGuide.rule2Body: The expensive work in a small business is rarely the thinking. It is the carrying: the same detail out of an email into a spreadsheet, out of the spreadsheet into a document, out of the document into another system. Nobody counts that as a task, which is why it appears in no report.
automationGuide.rule2Title: Automate the path the information takes, not the person
automationGuide.rule3Ask: When somebody sells you automation, ask where a person still decides. If no clear answer comes back, the answer is nowhere.
automationGuide.rule3Body: A system can prepare a draft without sending it. It can assemble an invoice without issuing it. That distinction is the most important part of any automation, and it is the part marketing material leaves out most often.
automationGuide.s1Body: The clearest case. The information already exists, it is just in the wrong place. There is no judgement here to replace.
automationGuide.s2Body: Quotations, confirmations, invoices. If nine in ten follow the same structure, the assembling is mechanical. The checking is not.
automationGuide.s2Title: Preparing documents from information you hold
automationGuide.s3Body: A system does not forget that a quotation has been open for eleven days. People forget that reliably, especially in good weeks.
automationGuide.s4Body: If three people have to be asked how far a job is, what is missing is not automation. It is a shared record of where things stand.
automationGuide.s5Body: Two tools that need to know the same thing. That is integration, rarely spectacular, and it saves minutes every day.
automationGuide.suitableLede: Work with these properties can be handed over reliably. It repeats, it has one clearly correct outcome, and a mistake shows up quickly and can be undone.
automationGuide.title: What should you automate first?
automationGuide.u1Body: Whether this customer deserves an exception. Whether this date will really hold. Rules can be written down, but the rule was never the reason for the decision.
automationGuide.u2Body: The rare case costs the most time and repays automation the least. Automate the nine ordinary cases and let the tenth stand out.
automationGuide.u3Body: A complaint, a delay, a conversation about price. A prepared draft helps. An automatically sent message damages the relationship faster than saying nothing would.
automationGuide.u4Body: Moving money, deleting something, committing to a date. The question is not whether the system can do it. It is what happens when it does it wrongly two hundred times overnight.
automationGuide.u5Body: If nobody can write down how a step works, it is not ready to be automated. It is ready for a conversation about what actually happens there.
automationGuide.unsuitableLede: Not out of caution, but because automation is worse at it. This work has no single correct outcome, or the mistake is expensive and cannot be taken back.
automationGuide.unsuitableTitle: What is better left with people

osStory.metaTitle: From a messy request to a reviewed quotation
osStory.metaDesc: One quotation, start to finish, in the system we run our own paperwork on: a loosely written email becomes a structured draft, and a person checks and saves it. Shown in a controlled test environment.
osStory.title: From a messy customer request to a reviewed quotation.
osStory.lede: This is the system we run our own quotations and invoices on. Below is one quotation, from the first email to the saved draft, exactly as it happens on screen.
osStory.disclosure: Demonstrated in a controlled Maxpromo test environment. The customer, the request and the company in it are invented. This is our own system at work, not a customer case study.
osStory.st1Body: A customer writes the way people write: a greeting, a remark about next week’s appointment, the three things they need, a signature. The email is pasted into the quotation screen as it is. Nobody retypes it.
osStory.st1Caption: The original email, pasted in. Nothing has been generated yet.
osStory.st1Alt: The quotation screen with an input window open. The pasted email lists three items: a switch cabinet conversion for a flat 2,400.00, testing of 48 portable devices at 12.50 each, and documentation for a flat 380.00.
osStory.st2Body: It reads the text and fills in the quotation: the customer, three positions, quantities and prices. The greeting, the appointment and the signature are left out. Then it checks its own result against the original and lists what it could not confirm, such as an incomplete address and a total the email never stated.
osStory.st2Caption: The filled form with the review notes the system raised. The customer was matched to the existing record.
osStory.st2Alt: The quotation form after extraction, with a list of review notes at the top, the customer Beckmann Elektrotechnik GmbH filled in, and a live preview showing three positions totalling 3,380.00 euros.
osStory.st3Body: At this point nothing has been saved. The form is a proposal. Someone reads the positions, checks them against what was asked for and decides whether it is right. Anything the system could not find in the original would be held here until a person deals with it.
osStory.st3Caption: Three positions and the total, before saving. The save button has not been pressed.
osStory.st3Alt: The quotation form scrolled to its positions: 2,400 flat, 48 pieces at 12.50 making 600.00, and 380 flat, with a total of 3,380.00 euros and the button “Angebot speichern” below. Bank details in the preview are covered.
osStory.st4Title: The draft becomes a business record.
osStory.st4Body: Only when the person saves does a record exist. The server issues the quotation number at that moment and stores the quotation as a draft. Sending it to the customer is a separate decision, taken later, by a person.
osStory.st4Caption: The saved quotation, in draft. It has not been sent.
osStory.st4Alt: The saved quotation ANG-2026-016 marked as draft, for Beckmann Elektrotechnik GmbH, with three positions and a total of 3,380.00 euros. The tax number in the footer is covered.
osStory.st5Body: The same system carries documents on through their life. An invoice is sent, then paid, and each state is recorded rather than remembered.
osStory.st5Caption: Invoices for the same invented customer, one sent and one paid.
osStory.st5Alt: The invoice list with two invoices for Beckmann Elektrotechnik GmbH: one marked sent, one marked paid.
osStory.redactionNote: In steps 3 and 4 our bank details and tax number are covered with black bars. Nothing else in any image has been changed.
osStory.ruleTitle: AI can prepare the work. People still make the business decision.
osStory.ruleBody: In this workflow the system creates nothing and sends nothing by itself. A person checks, saves and decides when to send.
osStory.scopeTitle: What this shows, and what it doesn’t.
osStory.shows1: A loosely written request can become a structured quotation without anyone retyping it.
osStory.shows2: The system says what it could not confirm instead of quietly filling the gap.
osStory.shows3: Saving, and later sending, stay decisions a person takes.
osStory.not1: How much time this saves. We haven’t measured it, so we don’t claim it.
osStory.not2: That every request comes out this cleanly. That is exactly why a person checks each one.
osStory.not3: Anything about a real customer. The customer here is invented.
osStory.ctaTitle: Does work arrive like this in your business?
osStory.ctaBody: If requests come in by email and get retyped into quotes, orders or tickets, show us how it happens today. We’ll tell you honestly whether a system like this would help.
